about: Twenty laws on the rates for hired work and on what a hired herdsman owes. First the yearly wages in grain: six kor for a ŠÀ.GUD, a worker whose title I cannot read and who may have to do with oxen (§258), and eight kor for a herdsman of cattle and sheep (§261), with fines for stealing a plough or one of two other farm implements whose names I cannot read (§259–260). §262 breaks off after a few words, and the next six lines of the column (xxxviii 31–36) are not preserved in Harper’s edition, so there is a gap. Then the herdsman’s duties (§263–267): he replaces an ox with an ox and a sheep with a sheep if he has lost them; if he has been paid and is content and still diminishes the herd, he pays the young and the yield by his contract; if he cheats and sells animals he is convicted and replaces tenfold; if a plague or a lion strikes the pen he clears himself before the god and the owner bears the loss; if he is careless he makes the damage good. The rest are day-rates: hired animals for threshing (§268–270), cattle with wagon and driver or the wagon alone (§271–272), a hired worker, dearer in the first half of the year (§273), skilled craftsmen by trade (§274, a list that is broken in the middle), and boats (§275–277). Several words are not readable from the grammar and I say so in the notes: ŠÀ.GUD, the two tools of §260, kazzatum and ḫiditum, lalâm, maḫirtum, most of the trade names of §274 and some verbs (uṣṣaḫḫir, ubbamma). Col. XXXVIII ends at line 101 and col. XXXIX is followed to line 57; Harper’s line numerals agree with his section headings throughout.

sentences.i: If a man has hired an ox-driver (?),
sentences.n: This part (§258–277) is the code’s tariff of hire for herdsmen, ploughmen, draught animals, threshers, wagons, hired workers and boats; most of the laws are one short condition and one price. They open with the usual šumma pattern: šumma awīlum … īgur “if a man has hired …”. īgur is the preterite of agārum “to hire”, here meaning “has hired” (as in §242). The man hired is written ŠÀ.GUD, two signs, a Sumerogram (a word written in Sumerian signs) that I cannot read in Akkadian; that he is some worker with oxen (an ox-driver, perhaps a ploughman) is only my guess, from the GUD “ox” inside the word and from §259, where a plough follows. So the word is left unread and marked uncertain.

sentences.i: he shall give him six kor of grain a year.
sentences.n: The price. 6 is the one sign for six; ŠE.GUR is two signs, “grain” and “kor” (the large measure of capacity, about 300 litres), written as Sumerograms with no ending; I say it kur šeʾam “a kor of grain”, with the number before it in the form that goes with a masculine noun (šeššet; reconstructed spoken form (?)). ina šattim 1 is “in the year, one”: MU (“year”) with no ending, then the numeral 1 and the sign KAM, which is silent after a numeral. inaddiššum is inaddin, the present of nadānum “to give”, plus -šum “to him”, with the final n of inaddin assimilated to the š of the suffix: “he shall give him”. As everywhere in the code, the present tense of the penalty means “shall”.

sentences.i: he shall pay five shekels of silver to the owner of the plough.

sentences.i: If he has stolen a GIŠ.APIN.TUK.KIN or a GIŠ.GAN.UR (two farm implements; unread),
sentences.n: No subject is written (šumma has no awīlum after it), so “he” means anyone. The two things stolen are Sumerograms I cannot read: GIŠ.APIN.TUK.KIN (wood-sign, plough-sign, TUK, KIN; Harper’s sign list gives the whole string as one entry under GIŠ) and GIŠ.GAN.UR (wood-sign, GAN, UR). They are plainly tools of the plough-team, since the penalty is three shekels, lower than for the plough itself, but what they are I do not know, and I do not translate them. I key the GAN sign as the plain gan sign (an uncertain identification) and the UR as the dog-sign. u lu is “or”: two words written together, ù “and” (the sign Ù) + lu “or” (the sign LU), as in §241–257. ištariq is the perfect of šarāqum, “has stolen”.

sentences.n: talittam is “the young (of the herd), the offspring” (talittum, from a root meaning “to bear”); umtaṭṭi is the D-stem perfect of maṭûm “to be few”, so “has reduced” (Harper’s um-ta-di; the sign di here stands for ṭi). ana pî riksātīšu is “according to the mouth of his contracts”: KA (mouth) is the Sumerogram for pûm “mouth, wording”, so ana pî means “according to the words of, as stated in”; riksātīšu is “his bindings, the terms of his contract” (riksum). The apodosis (the “then” part): talittam u biltam inaddin “he shall give the young and the yield”, i.e. what the herd should have produced (biltum is the yield, as in §26–41). The house rendering of ana pî ṣimdat šarrim (“according to the king’s schedule”) shows the same construction.

sentences.n: This law sets the herdsman’s duty when the herd is lost through no fault of his. tarbaṣim is the animal-pen or fold, written out syllabically, tar-ba-ṣi-im (Harper’s glossary: tarbaṣum “stable, fold”). lipit ilim is “a stroke of the god” (Harper’s glossary: liptu “stroke, visitation”, from lapātum “to touch”, so literally a touch), which I take to mean “plague, epidemic”; ittabši is “has occurred, has happened” (the perfect of bašûm, as in §112–126). I give “plague” with the literal sense beside it and mark it uncertain. UR.MAḪ is “lion” (house reading nēšum, §244); iddūk is the perfect of dâkum “to kill” (id-du-uk, with the doubled d, as in §244), here “has killed” (no object is written). Line 78 holds both the end of this condition and the start of the main clause, rēʾûm maḫar ilim, “the herdsman, before the god”: the herdsman is the subject of the oath-clearing in the next unit.

sentences.i: If a man hires a craftsman,
sentences.n: A list of daily wages for skilled workers (mār ummiānim, literally “a son of a craftsman”, as in §185–194; DUMU “son” and UM.MI.A, three signs). iggar (i-ig-ga-ar) is a present of agārum “to hire” (Harper lists it under the same verb): here the present, not the preterite īgur of the other laws; I do not know why this law changes the tense. Many of the trades are written with Sumerograms I cannot read, and the list is broken in the middle of the stone (the plate is hatched and the signs drawn in outline); where the signs are gone I show a gap.

sentences.i: If he has hired a maḫirtu (a kind of boat?; unread), her hire is 2½ grains of silver, and he shall pay it per day.
sentences.n: maḫirtum is the word met in §234–239 (elippum ša maḫirtim “a boat of the maḫirtum”): a kind of boat whose sense is unknown, left untranslated and marked UNCERTAIN (the hire here, like §275 and §277, is a boat’s, which is why I take it for a boat). No man is named as hirer: “he”. The price is II½ ŠE: the numeral 2 and the half-sign (𒈦, the same sign as maš) one after the other, said šinā u mišil “two and a half” (reconstructed spoken form (?)).

glossary.AT.KIT: AT.KIT, a Sumerogram of two signs, AT + KIT, a trade in the hire-list of §274, the amount lost; I cannot read it in Akkadian and leave it unread, UNCERTAIN · Sumerogram, reading not given
glossary.GA: GA(?), a single sign (GA) with the person-determinative {lu₂} and Harper’s own question mark, a trade in the hire-list of §274, the amount lost; the identification of the sign is Harper’s and doubtful, and the word is left unread, UNCERTAIN · Sumerogram, reading not given
glossary.GAB.A: GAB.A, a Sumerogram of two signs, GAB + A, with the person-determinative {lu₂} before it: the name of a craftsman or trade in the hire-list of §274, paid 5 še of silver a day; I cannot read it in Akkadian and leave it unread, UNCERTAIN · Sumerogram, reading not given
glossary.GIŠ.APIN.TUK.KIN: GIŠ.APIN.TUK.KIN, a Sumerogram of four signs, GIŠ + APIN + TUK + KIN, the name of a farm implement stolen with or beside the plough (§260); a compound of “plough” + TUK + KIN that I cannot read, left unread, UNCERTAIN · Sumerogram, reading not given
glossary.GIŠ.GAN.UR: GIŠ.GAN.UR, a Sumerogram of three signs, GIŠ + GAN + UR, the name of a second farm implement (§260), left unread, UNCERTAIN · Sumerogram, reading not given
glossary.GUL: GUL, a Sumerogram, a single sign with the person-determinative {lu₂}: a craftsman’s trade in the hire-list of §274, the amount lost; the sign means “to destroy, to hew”, and I do not read the word, UNCERTAIN · Sumerogram, reading not given
glossary.KAD: KAD, a Sumerogram, a single sign with the person-determinative {lu₂}: a craftsman’s trade in the hire-list of §274, paid 5 še a day (the numeral is restored by Harper, in brackets); the same sign is the second of NA.KAD “herdsman” (see nāqidum); I cannot read the word and leave it unread, UNCERTAIN · Sumerogram, reading not given
glossary.SA: SA, a Sumerogram, a single sign, a trade in the hire-list of §274, paid 4 še of silver a day (the numeral is restored in brackets, UNCERTAIN); the sign means “net, sinew, cord”, and the word is not read, UNCERTAIN · Sumerogram, reading not given
glossary.adi: up to, times: adi 12-šu “twelvefold” · as a conjunction, “as long as”, with the subjunctive: adi kirâm ṣabtu “as long as he holds the orchard” · adu 3-šu, adu 6-šu “three times, six times (as much)” — the multiplier, spelled a-du (Harper’s variant of adi; the plate has the sign DU) · adi šinīšu “up to his second time” = a second time (as adi 10-šu “tenfold”)
glossary.agrum: hired man, hireling: {amēlu}agram “a hireling” (the person-determinative + the sign Harper’s list reads agru) · {lu₂}NAGAR (§273): the sign NAGAR with the person-determinative, agram “a hireling” (accusative); Harper’s glossary gives the sign NAGAR two words, agru “hired man” (here) and nangaru “carpenter” (§274, see nangarum); a modern edition reads the hireling as ḪUN.GÁ
glossary.agārum: to hire: īgurma “he hired, and” · īgur (i-gur) “he hired”, without -ma, and īguru (i-gu-ru) “(who) hired”, with the relative -u: awīlum ša alpam īguru “the man who hired the ox” · īgur (i-gur) “he has hired”, the plain preterite of the hire-laws of §258–277 · iggar (i-ig-ga-ar) “he hires”, a present, Harper’s reading in §274 (the spelling with the extra i is not explained, UNCERTAIN)
glossary.alpum: ox (GU₄) · forms met: alpam (accusative, GU₄ alone or GU₄ + AM: GU₄-am), alpum (GU₄-um, subject), alpim (genitive, GU₄), alap (construct “ox of”: alap awīlim “a man’s ox”), alpīšu (GU₄-šu) “his ox”; the plate writes the word sometimes GU₄ alone and sometimes with a following sign
glossary.ana: to, for · with an infinitive, “to, for” (ana kirîm zaqāpim “to plant as an orchard”); “as” (ana kirîm), “into” (ana libbi), “at the rate of” (ana itêšu)
glossary.awīlum: man; the free citizen, the code’s first legal class
glossary.bašûm: to exist, arise: ibbaššû “which arose” · lā ibaššišum “there is not to him” (= he has none), with dative -šum · in broken forms …ši (ul ibašši, “there is not”, the verb itself restored); ibaššû “which are (there)”, in mimma ina qātīšu ibaššû · ibašši (i-ba-aš-ši, present) “there is, is upon”: ḫubullum elišu ibašši “a debt is upon him” · ittabši (it-tab-ši, perfect) “has happened, has broken out”, of the plague in the pen: lipit ilim ittabši “a stroke of the god has happened”
glossary.bašûm-Š: Š-stem of bašûm “to exist”: to bring into being, produce (a crop): uštabši “he has produced” (perfect) · uštabši (uš-tab-ši) “he has brought about” (perfect): kazzatam uštabši “he has brought about a harm (?)” · ušabšû (u-ša-ab-šu-u) “which he brought about” (preterite + relative -u)
glossary.biltum: yield, tribute, rent: nāši biltim “bearer of the yield”, the state tenant (spelled bi-il-tim, or carved with the tribute-sign GUN) · the produce of an orchard or field: biltam, bilat kirîm “the orchard’s yield”, bilat eqlim (written GÚN)
glossary.bānûm: creator; bānîšu “his creator” · builder (ŠITIM): bānûm “the builder”, bānîm šuāti “of that builder”, one who builds a house; the sign Harper numbers 168 is keyed ŠITIM tentatively, UNCERTAIN
glossary.bēlum: owner, lord: bēl ḫulqim “owner of the lost property” · owner of a field, bēl eqlim; bēl ḫubullim “creditor” · bēl kirîm “owner of the orchard” · bēl (be-el), the construct “owner of”, also with a suffix on the noun that follows: bēl ḫubullišu “his creditor”, bēl ḫubulliša “her creditor” · bēl (be-el, not the sign EN) “owner of”: bēl aššatim “the owner of the wife”, i.e. the man entitled to her (my reading) · bēlišu (be-li-šu) “its owner” (of an animal), bēlišuma “to its owner only” (with the emphatic -ma); bēl alpim “the owner of the ox” · bēl epinnim “the owner of the plough”, bēl tarbaṣim “the owner of the pen”; bēlīšunu (be-li-šu-nu) “their owners”, the owners of the cattle and sheep a herdsman has lost
glossary.dâkum: to kill; N-stem iddâk “he shall be killed” — the code’s death sentence · idukkū (i-du-uk-ku) “they shall kill” (active plural, unlike the N-stem iddâk) · iddūkšu (id-du-uk-šu) “has killed him/it”, taken as the perfect + -šu, the doubled d being the perfect’s infix -ta- assimilated to the root’s d (so read; UNCERTAIN in form) · iddūk (id-du-uk) “has killed”, of the lion in the pen, nēšum iddūk “a lion has killed”; the form is read as the perfect (iddūk with the infix -ta- assimilated, as in iddūkšu), not as the N-stem iddâk “he shall be killed”, UNCERTAIN in form
glossary.dīāšum: threshing: dīāšim (di-a-ši-im, genitive after ana) “for threshing”, said of hired animals (ox, donkey, a small animal) used to tread out the grain: ana dīāšim īgur “he has hired for threshing”; the infinitive of dâšum “to thresh”, used as a noun
glossary.ebēbum-D: D-stem of ebēbum “to be clean, pure”: to clear (of blame), declare clean: ubbamma (u-ub-ba-am-ma, D-stem + -ma) “he shall clear himself, and”, before the god; the sense is Harper’s, and the form is UNCERTAIN (I take it for the D-stem with the final b of the stem assimilated to the m of -ma, ubbab-ma > ubbamma; the spelling does not fit fully)
glossary.egûm: to be careless, neglect (Harper: “to be careless”): itēgi(ma) “he has been negligent, and” · igûma (i-gu-ma) “(who) was careless, and” (the preterite igi with the relative -u, as ilqû beside ilqe, then -ma) · īgīma (i-gi-ma, preterite + -ma) “he was careless, and”: malaḫum īgīma “the boatman was careless, and”
glossary.elippum: boat, ship (feminine; written with the Sumerogram GIŠ.MÁ, the two signs GIŠ and MÁ, with no ending written): elippum (nominative), elippam (accusative), elippim (genitive), elippi “boat of” (construct, before a genitive); elippišu (GIŠ.MÁ-šu) “his boat”, and elippušu (GIŠ.MÁ-šu, Harper’s elippu-šu) “his boat” as the subject of tebiat; the endings are the grammar’s · noun, Sumerogram
glossary.epinnum: plough (written with the Sumerogram GIŠ.APIN, the wood-determinative + APIN “plough”; Harper’s List no. 108): epinnam (accusative) “a plough”, epinnim (genitive) “of the plough”: bēl epinnim “the owner of the plough”; the case ending is supplied from the grammar, not written
glossary.idum: hire, wages (Harper: ID, the ideogram for hire): idi našpakim “the hire of the bin”, written with the single sign Á (A₂, “arm; hire”); the case ending is not written, so idi (construct, before a genitive) is an assumed reading, UNCERTAIN · idīšu (Á-šu, with -šu “his”) “his fee”, the physician’s pay: ana asîm idīšu “to the physician as his fee”; the case vowel is UNCERTAIN · Á alone, no ending and no suffix written, before a named kind of ox: idi GU₄.DA.UR.RA “the hire of a GU₄.DA.UR.RA”; the plate sign is Á (A₂), where Harper prints ID · idīša (Á-ša) “her hire”, idīšu (Á-šu) “its hire”, of a thing hired (a boat, an ox, a donkey), -ša / -šu agreeing with the thing; the case vowel is UNCERTAIN · idi (Á, construct) before a trade name: idi GAB.A “the hire of a GAB.A”, the hire-list of §274
glossary.ilum: god; here: the temple as owner · plural ilāni “gods” (written DINGIR.DINGIR, as in the litany): maḫar ilāni “before the gods”
glossary.ina: in, from · at (ina ebūrim “at harvest”); out of (ina bilat kirîm “out of the orchard’s yield”) · “through, by (means of)”: ina maḫāṣim “through beating”, ina pilšim “by a breach”; “regarding”: ina mimma ša … “regarding whatever …”; ina šanat “in the year” · “with, by”, of company or means (UNCERTAIN): ina liātim “with (or by) the cattle”
glossary.ištu: after, since; from; as a conjunction, “after, once”: ištu … īteliānim “after … have come up”
glossary.kaspum: silver — the code’s money, written KÙ.BABBAR “shining precious-metal” · kaspim: mišil mana kaspim “half a mina of silver” · with a spelled vowel after the logogram: KÙ.BABBAR-a-am, -i-im, -u-um: kaspam, kaspim, kaspum (accusative, genitive, nominative); kaspum as the subject; the grain-and-silver pair šeʾam u kaspam “grain and silver” · kasap (KÙ.BABBAR, no ending written) construct “silver of”: kasap tirḫatim “silver of the bride-price” · kaspi (KÙ.BABBAR, no complement written; Harper’s normalization) in kaspi mišil šīmišu “silver, half its price”
glossary.kazzatum: UNCERTAIN: kazzatam (ka-az-za-tam, accusative), kazzatim (genitive), a word for some harm or mishap in the pen brought about by a careless herdsman (Harper’s glossary: kazzatu “injury”); the spelling is ka + az + za + tam; “a harm (?)” is a guess from the sense of the clause, and the word is left as kazzatum
glossary.kurrum: the kor, a grain measure (written GUR; Harper: 300 KA): kur šeʾam “a kor of grain” · written GUR.É (the editors’ print GUR-É) as well as GUR: 1 GUR.É, kurrum “a kor” (UNCERTAIN: the .É is not explained here) · written ŠE.GUR.E, with a final E: ana 1 ŠE.GUR.E “for one kor (of grain)”; the .E is not explained here, UNCERTAIN
glossary.kânum-D: D-stem of kânum: to convict, prove against someone (uktīn, ukannūšuma) · uktīn (uk-ti-in, perfect, with the infixed -t-) “he has convicted”; ukannūšuma (u-ka-an-nu-šu-ma, present, plural, with -šu “him” and -ma) “they shall convict him, and”; ukānma (u-ka-an-ma, present, singular) “he shall convict, and” · ukannūšima (u-ka-an-nu-ši-ma) “they shall convict her, and”, present plural with -ši “her” and -ma
glossary.kīma: like, as · as, like; with a verb in the subjunctive: kīma ubbalu “as he brings (it)” · according to: kīma ṣimdat šarrim “according to the king’s schedule” · “since, when”, before a stative: kīma mimmûšu lā ḫalqu “since his goods are not lost” · “in proportion to”: kīma emūq zittiša “in proportion to the strength of her share”, kīma emūq bīt abim “in proportion to the means of her father’s house” · in place of, for (of animal for animal): alpam kīma alpim “an ox for an ox” (the §263 restitution)
glossary.lalûm: UNCERTAIN: LÁ-am, lalâm (accusative), a hired animal in the threshing rates beside the ox and the donkey, hired for 1 qa of grain; written LÁ (the sign “to hang, to weigh”) + AM, read lalâm; Harper’s glossary has “small animal, goat (?)”, which fits the very low price, but the word is not certain
glossary.libbum: heart · ana libbi “into”: ana libbi zittišu “into his share” · libbaša, libbiša (li-ib-ba-ša, li-ib-bi-ša) “her heart”: mala libbiša “as much as her heart wants”; libbaša uṭabbū “they shall make her heart good”, i.e. content her · ša libbiša (li-ib-bi-ša) “what is in her womb”, literally “that of her heart”, the unborn child: ana ša libbiša “for what was in her womb”
glossary.liptum: a touch, stroke, blow (from lapātum “to touch”; Harper’s glossary: liptu “stroke, visitation”): lipit (li-bi-it, with BI read as pi, construct) ilim “a stroke of the god”, a plague or sickness sent by the god among the herd, taken here as a sudden affliction (?); the form lipit is a construct before ilim, UNCERTAIN in meaning (“plague”)
glossary.liātum: cattle: Harper’s LID.GUD.ZUN — the cow-sign, the ox-sign, and the plural marker (the stele carves ḪI+A)
glossary.lū: or; either (lū … lū “whether … or”); with verb: “let …” · ù lu, two words written together, “or”: ù lu ina maḫāṣim “or through beating”
glossary.maḫar: before, in the presence of: maḫar ilim “before the god”
glossary.maḫirtum: UNCERTAIN: a kind of boat, sense unknown: maḫirtim (ma-ḫi-ir-tim, genitive; Harper restores part of the word in §240): ša maḫirtim “the one of the maḫirtu”, elippum ša maḫirtim “a boat of the maḫirtu” · noun, sense uncertain · maḫirtam (ma-ḫi-ir-tam, accusative), the object of īgur in §276: šumma maḫirtam īgur “if he has hired a maḫirtu”
glossary.maḫārum: to receive: imḫur(u) · imḫur, imḫuru “he received” (preterite; subjunctive in a clause), imaḫḫar “he shall receive” (present); …ḫari… in a broken form · to face, withstand (litany): qabal lā maḫārim “combat none can face” · imtaḫar (im-ta-ḫar) “she received” (perfect; Harper’s maḫāru I,2, “to receive”): grain and silver for beer · maḫir (ma-ḫi-ir, stative, 3rd singular) “has received”: idīšu … maḫir “he has received his wage” · imaḫḫaršu (i-maḫ-ḫar-šu, present + -šu) “he shall accept from him”: the owner of the pen imaḫḫaršu the loss, “shall accept it from him”
glossary.maṭûm-D: D-stem of maṭûm “to be little”: to reduce, diminish: umtaṭṭi (perfect) “he has reduced”
glossary.miqittum: loss, fall, what has fallen: miqitti (mi-qi₂-it-ti, construct) “the loss of” (the KI of the spelling is read qi), from maqātum “to fall”: miqitti tarbaṣim “the loss of the pen”, the animals lost to the plague or the lion; the sign values are mi-qi₂-it-ti
glossary.murteddûm: driver, one who drives (the cattle and the wagon): murteddīša (mu-ur-te-di-ša, with the suffix -ša “its”) “its driver”, taken as a participle of redûm “to lead, drive” in the Gt-stem (the infix -t- after the first radical), UNCERTAIN in the stem; the cattle, the wagon and its driver are hired together at the higher day-rate
glossary.mārum: son (DUMU) — here: a minor, not yet able to sell · member of a group: mārū ugārim (DUMU A.GÀR{meš}) “the sons of the irrigated land”, the district’s farmers · mār awīlim “a man’s son” (DUMU); mārī (DUMU{meš}) “sons” (oblique plural, which may include daughters, so “children”); māršu (DUMU-šu) “his son” · mārūša (DUMU{meš}-ša) “her sons” (nominative plural + suffix); mārīša (DUMU-ša) “her son” (genitive + suffix): ana mārīša “to her son” · mārī (DUMU-i) “my son” (-ī “my”); mārī (DUMU{meš}) “children” in mārī ūlissum “children she bore him”; mārū (DUMU{meš}) “sons” as subject: mārū ana ummātim ul izuzzū “the sons shall not divide by mothers” · mār X (DUMU, the sign TUR) “a member of the class X”, literally “son of X”: mār ummiānim “a craftsman”, mār zinništim “the son of a woman”; māram (DUMU) “a son”, mārašu (DUMU-šu) “his son”, mārī (DUMU{meš}) “sons”, mārīšu “his sons”
glossary.nadānum: to give, pay: inaddin, iddinam, iddinušum; nadānim “to give” · iddin “he gave”; ana kaspim nadānum “to sell”: inaddinūma (present, plural) “they shall sell, and …” · iddin, iddinu “he gave” (preterite; the subjunctive -u in a ša- or inūma clause); iddinma “he gave, and”; …in, …din in broken forms; inaddin “he shall give”: ana damqaršu inaddin “he shall give to his merchant” · ittadinma (it-ta-di-in-ma) “he has given, and” (perfect); inaddinu (i-na-ad-di-nu) “(which) he gives” (present, with the subjunctive -u) · ittandin (it-ta-an-di-in, perfect with an extra -n-) “he has handed over”: ana kiššātim ittandin “he handed over into service”; ittadin (it-ta-din) “he has given”, i.e. sold; ana maṣṣarūtim inaddin “he gives for safekeeping”; iddinūšumma “they gave him, and” · inaddin also of a woman, “she shall give” · inaddišši (i-na-ad-di-iš-ši) “he/she shall give her” (the n of the stem swallowed before -ši), of a sale: ana kaspim inaddišši “she may sell her”, ul inaddišši “she shall not sell her” · anaddin “I shall give”, with the n merged into the k of -kum: anaddikkum (a-na-ad-di-ik-kum) “I shall give (her) to you”; iddinu (id-di-nu) “(which) he gave”; iddinušum “he gave him” · nadānam (na-da-nam, infinitive accusative) “to give”: warkassa … nadānam “(that she may) give her estate” · iddišši (id-di-iš-ši) “he gave her”, preterite + -ši, the n written š: ana mutim iddišši “he gave her to a husband” · inaddinūši (i-na-ad-di-nu-ši) “they shall give her”, inaddinūšimma (i-na-ad-di-nu-šim-ma) “they shall give her, and”, ittadnūšimma (it-ta-ad-nu-ši-im-ma) “they have given her, and” (perfect plural + -šim + -ma) · iddinušim (id-di-nu-ši-im) “he gave her”, with the subjunctive -u in a ša-clause · inaddiššum (i-na-ad-di-iš-šum) “he shall give him” (inaddin + -šum, the n assimilated to š) · innadnušum (in-na-ad-nu-šum) “were given to him” (N-stem preterite + relative -u + -šum): ša innadnušum “that was given to him” · ittadin (it-ta-di-in) “he has given” (perfect): ana kaspim ittadin “he has sold for silver”
glossary.nakārum-D: D-stem of nakārum “to be strange, different”: to make different, change: uttakkir (ut-ta-ak-ki-ir, D perfect) “he has changed”: šimtam uttakkir “he has changed the mark (?)” (the object is UNCERTAIN; the verb is plain from the stem)
glossary.nangarum: carpenter, joiner (written with the single sign NAGAR; Harper’s glossary gives the sign two words, nangaru “carpenter” and agru “hired man”): nangarim (nan-garim, genitive, as Harper prints it; the plate has NAGAR alone) “of a carpenter”, in the hire-list of §274: idi … nangarim 4 še kaspim “the hire of a … carpenter, 4 grains of silver”; the same sign with the person-determinative is Harper’s agrum “hireling” in §273 (see agrum), and the two readings are told apart by the context only; Harper’s form is kept (a later normalization of the carpenter is naggārum)
glossary.nāqidum: herdsman, keeper of flocks (written NA.KAD, the signs NA + KAD, as Harper’s glossary gives it; the identification of the sign group is old and may be superseded): nāqidam (accusative, no ending written) “a herdsman”, hired ana LID.GUD.ZUN u ṣênê rīm “to pasture cattle and sheep”; the case ending is supplied
glossary.nēšum: lion — written with the two signs UR “dog” + MAḪ “great”: UR.MAḪ, said nēšum; labbum is also “lion” and the signs do not choose between them, UNCERTAIN which word is meant: ina ṣērim UR.MAḪ “a lion in the open country”
glossary.pûm: mouth (the KA sign); ina pī mātim “in the mouth of the land” · ana pî ṣimdat šarrim “according to the mouth of the king’s ordinance” · ana pî riksātīšu “according to his contract”, literally “to the mouth of his binding terms” (KA read pî)
glossary.qûm: the qa, a capacity measure of about a litre (Harper: QA), written with the sign SÌLA: ḫamšat qa šeʾim “five qa of grain”; the identification of the plate’s sign as SÌLA is the editor’s, UNCERTAIN
glossary.ramānum: self: ramānšu ipaddar “he shall redeem himself” · ana ramānīša (ra-ma-ni-ša) “by itself, for itself”, of the wagon hired alone: ṣumbamma ana ramānīša “the wagon only, by itself”
glossary.rêʾûm-pasture: to pasture, graze (a herd): the infinitive in the genitive after ana, ana … rēʾîm “to pasture” (ri-im), said rēʾîm; the spelling ri-im is Harper’s and the reading of the word as the infinitive of rêʾûm (the verb behind rēʾûm “shepherd”) is my own from the grammar, UNCERTAIN
glossary.rēšum: head, top · rēš šattim (ri-eš ša-at-tim) “the start of the year”, literally “the head of the year”: ištu rēš šattim “from the start of the year”
glossary.rēʾûm: shepherd — here written with the Sumerogram SIPA · herdsman of cattle and sheep, the hired man of §264–267, written SIPA: rēʾûm “the herdsman” (rēʾûm, in the lost-herd laws); the signs are the same as for “shepherd”, and the Akkadian says herdsman as well
glossary.taktida: UNCERTAIN: ta-ak-ti-da, a word after adi “until” in the rate of the hired man, ištu rēš šattim adi ḫamšim warḫim … ištu šeššim warḫim adi taktida šattim “from the start of the year until the fifth month … from the sixth month until the taktida of the year”; I take it as a word for the end of the year (“the close, the end (?)”) from the context and do not know the form; left unread
glossary.talittum: young, offspring (of the herd), from walādum “to bear”: talittam (ta-li-id-tam, accusative) “the young”, the increase of the flock, owed with the biltum “yield”: talittam u biltam inaddin “he shall give the young and the yield”; the stem w of walādum is lost in the noun
glossary.tarbaṣum: cattle-pen, fold: tarbaṣim (tar-ba-ṣi-im, genitive and after ina) “(in) the pen”: ina tarbaṣim “in the pen”; bēl tarbaṣim “the owner of the pen”; miqitti tarbaṣim “the loss of the pen”; the sign ṣi is the one Harper numbers 72, keyed ZI
glossary.ugārum: the irrigated farmland of a district, the commons (written A.GÀR): ugāram, ugārim; mārū ugārim (DUMU A.GÀR{meš}) “the sons of the irrigated land”, the farmers of the district
glossary.ummiānum: a craftsman, a skilled worker (written with the Sumerograms UM.MI.A, three signs UM, MI, A, with no ending written): ummiānim “of a craftsman” (genitive, read from the context); mār ummiānim “a craftsman”, literally “a son of a craftsman” (see mārum) · noun, Sumerogram
glossary.warḫum: month (written with ITI, the moon-month sign): warḫim “of the month”
glossary.ŠÀ.GUD: ŠÀ.GUD, a Sumerogram of two signs, ŠÀ + GUD, a worker hired for a yearly wage of grain, whose Akkadian name I cannot read; “ox-driver, ploughman” is only a guess from the signs (ŠÀ “heart, inside” + GUD “ox”) and from the plough that follows in §259, UNCERTAIN · Sumerogram, reading not given
glossary.šalāmum-D: D-stem of šalāmum “to be whole, sound”: to make good, restore (Harper: “to restore”): ušallamma (u-ša-lam-ma) “he shall make good, and”
glossary.šarāqum: to steal: išriq · išriqma (iš-ri-iq-ma, preterite + -ma) “he stole, and”
glossary.šattum: year: šattam (syllabic, §31) or MU (the year-sign, §30) · šattim (genitive); plural šanātim “years” (ša šanātim “of the years”); MU 4{kam}, said erbe šanātim “four years” · MU 3{kam}, said šalāš šanātim “for three years”; šanat (ša-na-at) “(in) the year”, ina šanat “each year”
glossary.šeššum: sixth: šeššim (ši-ši-im, genitive, before ITI “month”), šeššim warḫim “the sixth month”, the start of the second period of the year; from the numeral šeššet “six”
glossary.šeʾum: barley, grain (the ŠE sign) · ŠE-am, ŠE-im, ŠE-um, written with the logogram and a spelled vowel; šeʾum as the subject; ŠE-am-ma “grain only” (with the restricting -ma); in broken forms še… · ŠE alone, as a small silver weight, the še “grain”, one hundred and eightieth of a shekel: 5 ŠE kaspim “five še of silver”, the day-rates of §273–277
glossary.šimtum: mark, brand (?): šimtam (ši-im-tam, accusative) “the mark”, in šimtam uttakkir “he has changed the mark”, a herdsman altering the brand of the animals before selling them; the sense “mark” is UNCERTAIN, taken from the context, and may be the same word as šīmtum “fate, what is fixed”; the spelling does not show the vowel length
glossary.šiqlum: shekel — the basic weight of silver, about 8.3 g (written GÍN): 2 šiqil kaspim
glossary.šumma: if — the word that opens every law of the code
glossary.šuššum: one-sixth (written IGI.6.GAL, “the sixth part”): šuššum “a sixth”; in the silver rate it is followed by 6 še, “one-sixth and 6 grains” (IGI.6.GAL šeššet šeʾam) · šuššat (IGI.6.GAL, before kaspim) “one sixth”, of a shekel of silver; the unit is not written, and the spoken form is reconstructed, UNCERTAIN
glossary.ūmum: day; ūmišu “daily” (written UD-mi-šu) · plural “days”: ūmī (written UD-mi-) “days”: ina ūmīšu lā malûtim “in his days not full” (the days of a lease) · ūm “day” (UD), before a following word, in ūm NER lā “a day (when ?) NER not …” · ūmīšu (UD-mi-šu) “his days”: ūmīšu imannûma “they shall count his days” · ina ūmim (i-na UD) “per day, by the day”, with the numeral 1{kam}: ina ūmim 1{kam} 180 qa “for each day 180 qa”; the day-rate formula of §271–277
glossary.ḫalāqum-D: D-stem of ḫalāqum “to be lost, to perish”: to destroy, cause to be lost: uḫalliqu (preterite, with the relative -u) “(the grain) he destroyed” · uḫtalliq (uḫ-ta-al-li-iq, perfect, 3rd singular) “he has destroyed”: šumma makkūr uḫtalliq “if he has destroyed property”; of a boatman, ù lū uḫtalliq “or has destroyed (it)”
glossary.ḫamšum: fifth: ḫamšim (ḫa-am-ši-im, genitive, before ITI “month”), ḫamšim warḫim “the fifth month”, the end of the first period of the year in the hired man’s rates
glossary.ḫarratum: UNCERTAIN, not read: ḫarratim (ḫar-ra-tim, after a damaged stretch) in the herdsman’s wage clause: idīšu … ḫarratim maḫir “has received his wage … ḫarratim”; Harper marks this word and the mimma before it with his own (?), the stone is damaged here, and I do not know the word, so the unit leaves the damaged phrase untranslated; the lemma is only a placeholder for Harper’s spelling
glossary.ḫiditum: UNCERTAIN: ḫidit (ḫi-di-it, construct) “the … of”, followed by kazzatim: the “loss (?)” the herdsman must make good; Harper’s glossary has a word “blame, reproach, disaster, loss” for it; the meaning is guessed from the parallel with miqitti in §266, and the word is left as ḫiditum
glossary.ṣarārum-D: UNCERTAIN: uṣarrirma (u-ṣa-ar-ri-ir-ma, D-stem preterite + -ma) “he has been dishonest (?), and”, of the herdsman who cheats; taken as a D-stem of ṣarārum “to be dishonest” (Harper’s glossary: ṣarāru II, “to be dishonest”) from the sense of the law (he changes the mark and sells the animals), not certain
glossary.ṣeḫērum-D: D-stem (?) of ṣeḫērum “to be small”: to make small, diminish (the herd): uṣṣaḫḫir (uz-za-aḫ-ḫi-ir, with uz- for uṣ-) “he has diminished”: liātim uṣṣaḫḫir ṣēnī uṣṣaḫḫir “he has made the cattle fewer, he has made the sheep fewer”; the identification is UNCERTAIN, from the grammar and the sense next to maṭûm-D “to reduce”; the form fits a D-stem only loosely, and Harper’s glossary lists it under an intransitive stem, “to be diminished”, which would make the animals the ones that dwindle
glossary.ṣumbum: wagon, cart: ṣumbam (GIŠ.MAR.GÍD.DA, accusative), ṣumbamma (GIŠ.MAR.GÍD.DA-ma, accusative + -ma) “the wagon only”, a Sumerogram of four signs (GIŠ + MAR + GÍD + DA, “long wagon”) read in Akkadian; the sign GÍD is keyed LAL, tentative; ṣumbum is my reading of the Sumerogram from its sense (a hired wagon with its driver), UNCERTAIN
glossary.ṣēnum: sheep, the flock: ṣēnē over the sheep-sign LU · also written U₈.UDU{ḫi.a} (ewe + sheep + plural marker): ṣēnū, ṣēnī
glossary.ṭābum: to be good, pleasing: ṭāb (ṭa-ab, stative, 3rd singular) “is good”: libbašu ṭāb “his heart is good”, i.e. he is satisfied, content
